claims.text: Scandinavian vampires, called einherjar or vargr, are Embraced for courage, hardiness and ferocity, and keep the old ways while gathering warriors who will not bow to Christendom.
They make homes in frozen woods and lonely isles, and some still sail the sea lanes; when the sun sets for the whole northern winter, they raid by darkness for glory, gold and blood.
Vargr society has a strange democracy of its own and fierce loyalty to its jarls.

title: Thralls of the North
summary: Bondsmen in Norse society and their use to the einherjar.

claims.text: Norse thralls are property with no blood price, though their owners can claim compensation; their children are born thralls, and freedom can be granted or bought.
Thralls serve as the occasional human sacrifice and as food for hungry einherjar, and a vampire with silver can simply buy them from a farmer.
Anyone can fall into thralldom through debt, war or shipwreck; slavery fades quickly in Iceland and ends in Scandinavia with Christianity.

title: Norse Faith and the Second Sight
summary: How the Norse see their gods and fate.

claims.text: To ordinary Norse the Aesir and Vanir are distant, fearsome warriors to be appeased and emulated, not powers behind daily life; even the gods cannot escape the fate the Norns decree.
A Norse seer with the second sight perceives spirits, talks with them and traces the Norns' threads of fate, but also foresee their own unavoidable deaths.
The faithful among the Norse revere all the gods, even when honouring one patron above the rest.

title: Assamites and Brujah of the North
summary: Two clans among the Norse vampires.

claims.text: A few Norse raiders in the Middle East from the 700s, or Varangian guards in Constantinople, may have been Embraced by Assamites; such vampires hunt the vargr and jarls of the North.
Norse who do not take up the clan's beliefs make Khayyin a giant, a jotun, who tricked Haquim and stole the power to make false einherjar.
After the Gangrel, the Brujah are probably the most common Norse vampires, found mostly in new trading towns such as Bergen and Schleswig; the bond of jarl and huskarl reminds them of lost Carthage.
